prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- British TV channels could advertise abortion services for the first time under new advertising rules proposed Thursday by an ad industry group. The new proposals will also allow condoms to be advertised more widely on television. The Broadcast Committee of Advertising Practice, the industry body responsible for writing and enforcing advertising rules in Britain, said the commercials would be for pregnancy advisory services that give information about a range of options to pregnant women, including abortion. If an organization does not offer information about abortion, it would have to make that clear in the ad, BCAP spokeswoman Lynsay Taffe said. Abortion clinics, which require referrals from doctors or hospitals, would not be allowed to advertise under the proposed rules, Taffe said. There would be no restrictions on when such ads could air on British television, she said, but programmers would have to keep the sensitive topic in mind and not schedule the ads around religious programs, for example. "It's a sensitive product, so it would have to be scheduled sensitively," Taffe told CNN. The proposal is among a number of updates to current advertising standards that the Committee for Advertising Practice and BCAP, its broadcasting arm, published Thursday after an 18-month review. "Each year the British public (sees) millions of advertisements, many of which are memorable," the committee said. "The advertising codes aim to make sure that they are memorable for the right reasons." The public now has until June 19 to comment on the proposals before they come into force, likely in 2010, the committee said. The new proposals also contain a change on advertising condoms on television. Under current rules, condoms generally cannot be advertised on TV before 9 p.m. in order to protect younger viewers, the committee said. New rules would relax the restrictions on advertising condoms, with the only requirement that they not be shown around programs intended for children younger than 10. The change came after Joyce Gould, a member of the House of Lords, requested the change and noted that Britain had the highest teenage pregnancy rate in Europe along with spiraling rates of sexually transmitted diseases, the committee said. Gould reported a survey that showed young people believed TV was one of the most effective ways of encouraging them to use condoms. "The presence of condom advertisements on television continues to be a subject of complaint to the (Advertising Standards Authority), but numbers are very low," the committee said. "Nevertheless, BCAP has to balance public sensitivities against a public health problem that is clearly urgent."

LONDON, England (CNN) — Proposed changes to Britain’s advertising regulations could permit television networks to promote abortion-related advisory services for the first time, an advertising industry organization announced Thursday. The plans would also expand the circumstances in which condom commercials may be broadcast.

The Broadcast Committee of Advertising Practice, which drafts and enforces UK broadcast advertising standards, said the proposed commercials would promote pregnancy counseling organizations that explain the various choices available to pregnant women, including abortion.

BCAP spokeswoman Lynsay Taffe said any organization that does not provide abortion information would be required to state that clearly in its advertisement. Clinics that perform abortions would remain barred from advertising because patients must be referred to them by a doctor or hospital.

Taffe said the commercials would not be subject to specific time restrictions. However, broadcasters would need to consider the sensitive nature of the subject when scheduling them and, for instance, avoid placing them near religious programming.

“It's a sensitive product, so it would have to be scheduled sensitively,” she told CNN.

The abortion-advertising proposal is one of several revisions unveiled Thursday by the Committee for Advertising Practice and its broadcast division, BCAP, following an 18-month examination of existing standards.

“Each year the British public (sees) millions of advertisements, many of which are memorable,” the committee said. “The advertising codes aim to make sure that they are memorable for the right reasons.”

Members of the public have until June 19 to submit feedback. The committee said the revised rules would probably take effect in 2010.

The proposals would also loosen the current limits on television advertising for condoms. Existing regulations generally prohibit condom commercials before 9 p.m. to shield younger audiences. Under the proposed system, such advertisements could be shown earlier, provided they are not placed around programs aimed at children under age 10.

The committee said the revision followed a request from House of Lords member Joyce Gould, who pointed to Britain’s status as having Europe’s highest teenage pregnancy rate, as well as sharply increasing rates of sexually transmitted diseases. Gould also cited survey findings indicating that young people regarded television as one of the most effective tools for persuading them to use condoms.

“The presence of condom advertisements on television continues to be a subject of complaint to the (Advertising Standards Authority), but numbers are very low,” the committee said. “Nevertheless, BCAP has to balance public sensitivities against a public health problem that is clearly urgent.”

Britain’s advertising regulators have proposed changes to television advertising rules that could allow pregnancy advisory services to discuss abortion in broadcast advertisements for the first time. The proposals follow an 18-month review of the advertising code and are intended to improve public access to information about sexual and reproductive health services.

Under the proposed rules, organizations offering pregnancy advice would be permitted to advertise on television, including services that provide information about abortion or refer women to abortion providers. Advertisements would, however, have to state clearly what services the organization offers. This requirement is intended to ensure that viewers can distinguish between providers offering a full range of pregnancy options and groups that do not provide or arrange abortion services.

The regulators also proposed relaxing existing restrictions on condom advertising. Condom commercials could be shown more widely, although broadcasters would still have to schedule them sensitively and take account of the likely age and composition of the audience. Restrictions would remain around programming primarily directed at younger children, while the content and presentation of advertisements would continue to be governed by standards of taste, responsibility and child protection.

Supporters of the changes are likely to argue that broader advertising could help reduce unintended pregnancies and sexually transmitted infections by making reliable information and services easier to find. Television campaigns could also reach people who might not otherwise seek advice from health professionals, schools or specialist organizations.

The proposals may nevertheless prove controversial. Abortion remains a politically and morally sensitive subject, and critics may object to its inclusion in television advertising or question whether commercial pregnancy services should be promoted in this way. Clear disclosure rules are therefore a central part of the plan, particularly where an advertiser has a religious, ethical or campaigning position that affects the options it provides.

The changes are not yet final. They will be subject to public and industry consultation before regulators decide whether to incorporate them into the broadcasting advertising code. If adopted, they would mark a significant shift in British television policy, potentially introducing abortion-related advertising to the medium for the first time and allowing condom promotion across a wider range of programming.

Overall, the proposals seek to balance greater access to sexual-health information with safeguards for children and other potentially sensitive audiences. Their adoption would substantially broaden the ways in which pregnancy advice, abortion information and contraception can be presented to the British public.

# Britain considers easing TV advertising rules for abortion services, condoms

**LONDON** — British regulators are considering changes to television advertising rules that could allow abortion providers to promote their services and permit condom commercials to be shown earlier in the evening.

Under the proposed rules, organizations offering abortion services could advertise on television for the first time, provided the commercials complied with standards on accuracy, social responsibility and protection of young viewers.

Condom advertisements could also be broadcast before the traditional 9 p.m. “watershed,” although restrictions would remain around programs aimed at younger children.

Supporters say the changes would give viewers better access to information about sexual health and pregnancy services, particularly as many people may not know where to seek professional advice.

Critics, including some religious and anti-abortion groups, argue that television advertising could present abortion as a routine commercial service and expose children to sensitive material.

Regulators say any advertisements would be subject to strict content rules. Commercials could not be misleading, exploit fear or distress, or make irresponsible claims. Broadcasters would also be expected to consider the likely audience and the context in which an advertisement appeared.

The proposals are part of a broader review intended to modernize Britain’s advertising code and reflect changes in public health policy and social attitudes. They would not automatically permit unrestricted advertising: individual commercials would still require approval, and scheduling limits could apply.

A public consultation and further regulatory review would take place before any final rules were adopted.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the Broadcast Committee of Advertising Practice’s proposed changes to UK television advertising standards, including rules for pregnancy advisory services, abortion-related ads, and condom commercials.
counterfactuals.output:
## BCAP proposals on UK television advertising standards

The Broadcast Committee of Advertising Practice (BCAP), which writes the rules enforced by the Advertising Standards Authority for television and radio advertising, proposed a significant revision of the UK Broadcast Advertising Code as part of its 2009 review. The changes were intended to reflect developments in health policy, sexual-health education and broadcasting since the previous code was written.

### Pregnancy advisory and abortion-related services

BCAP proposed allowing **post-conception pregnancy advisory services—including organisations that arrange or provide abortions—to advertise on television and radio**. This would remove the effective prohibition that had prevented commercial abortion providers from broadcasting advertisements.

The proposed rules would not give providers unrestricted freedom. Advertisements would still have to:

- comply with general requirements on legality, accuracy, harm, offence and social responsibility;
- avoid misleading claims or exploiting women who may be distressed or vulnerable;
- comply with relevant medical and health-service regulation; and
- avoid presenting abortion or other pregnancy outcomes irresponsibly.

A particularly important transparency rule concerned organisations that offer pregnancy counselling but **do not provide or refer women for abortion**. Their advertisements would have to make that limitation clear. BCAP’s rationale was that viewers seeking impartial pregnancy advice should not be misled about the nature or ideological position of the service.

The proposal was often described in press coverage as permitting “abortion advertising,” but it was more precisely a change allowing regulated pregnancy and termination-service providers to advertise their services—not a relaxation of the law governing abortion itself.

### Condom advertising

BCAP also proposed removing the general rule that confined condom commercials largely to the post-watershed period. Under the old arrangements, condom advertisements were generally restricted until after 9 p.m., with a separate earlier allowance on Channel 4.

The revised approach would permit condom advertising earlier in the day, while protecting young children through programme-placement restrictions. Such advertisements would not be permitted in or around programming:

- made principally for children, or
- likely to appeal particularly to children below the specified age threshold, generally under ten.

Condom commercials would also remain subject to rules on taste, sexual imagery, harm and offence. Thus, the proposal changed scheduling rather than authorising explicit sexual content.

BCAP argued that the change could support public-health objectives, including reducing sexually transmitted infections and unintended pregnancy, and reflected the fact that condoms are a lawful, widely available health product.

### Controversy and status

The proposals attracted strong disagreement. Sexual-health organisations and abortion-rights groups generally welcomed greater access to factual information and the requirement that pregnancy advisers disclose whether they offered abortion referrals. Religious and anti-abortion groups argued that television advertising could normalise or commercialise abortion and objected to allowing condom advertisements before the watershed.

These measures were initially **consultation proposals**, not immediate changes in the law. Following consultation and revision, the new UK broadcast advertising code took effect in 2010. The underlying approach was to permit more health and sexual-health advertising while relying on transparency, content controls and child-focused scheduling restrictions rather than blanket bans.

## BCAP proposals would reshape broadcast rules on abortion and condom advertising

Proposed changes to the UK’s broadcast advertising rules would allow greater freedom to advertise pregnancy-advice services and condoms on television and radio. The Broadcast Committee of Advertising Practice (BCAP), which writes the rules enforced by the Advertising Standards Authority, said the revisions were intended to reflect changes in public health policy and society while retaining safeguards for children and other potentially vulnerable audiences.

### Advertising pregnancy and abortion services

One of the most contentious proposals concerns organisations offering advice about unplanned pregnancies. The changes would permit appropriately regulated services—including those that provide or arrange abortions—to advertise on television and radio.

The proposals are better understood as rules for advertising pregnancy-advice services rather than for promoting abortion itself. Advertisements would still have to be legal, accurate and responsible. They could not mislead viewers about the nature of the service or exploit fear, distress or vulnerability. Providers that do not offer or refer women for abortion could also be required to make the limits of their service clear.

BCAP nevertheless recognised that abortion is a sensitive and strongly contested subject. As a result, such advertising would require careful scheduling. Restrictions would be intended to prevent advertisements from appearing alongside programmes aimed at children or in contexts where they could cause particular distress or serious offence.

Sensitive scheduling does not mean that an advertisement is automatically unsuitable for all viewers before the 9pm watershed. Rather, broadcasters would have to consider the likely audience, the programme’s subject matter and the tone of the advertisement. A factual notice giving contact details for a regulated pregnancy service, for example, would be treated differently from graphic, alarming or overtly campaigning material.

### Why condom advertising rules could be relaxed

BCAP also proposed widening the times at which condom advertisements could be shown. Traditional restrictions had largely confined such advertising to later evening schedules, limiting its ability to reach some sexually active teenagers and young adults.

The case for change was driven in part by continuing concern about the UK’s levels of teenage pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections. Public-health bodies argued that condoms are not merely ordinary commercial products: they are an important means of reducing unintended pregnancy and the transmission of infections.

Under the proposed approach, condom advertisements could be broadcast earlier, while remaining subject to restrictions around programmes made for or especially attractive to younger children. The aim was to make responsible sexual-health messages more visible to teenagers without placing sexualised advertising in clearly inappropriate settings.

### Balancing protection and public health

The two proposals illustrate BCAP’s attempt to move away from broad prohibitions and towards more targeted regulation. In both cases, the committee sought to balance competing concerns: protecting children, avoiding misleading or offensive material, respecting audience sensitivities and ensuring that people can obtain information about lawful health services.

Supporters argued that the changes could help viewers make informed choices and allow public-health messages to reach those most at risk. Critics feared that earlier condom advertising might sexualise childhood, while abortion-related advertising could trivialise a profound decision or expose audiences to material they find morally troubling.

The proposals would not create an unrestricted right to advertise either service. Advertisers would still have to meet strict standards on accuracy, responsibility and presentation, and broadcasters would remain responsible for placing advertisements appropriately. The central change would be to permit more information while relying on content controls and sensitive scheduling rather than blanket bans.

counterfactuals.output:
**LONDON — Britain’s broadcast-advertising regulator is reviewing rules that could, for the first time, allow commercial pregnancy-advice services to promote themselves on television and radio, while maintaining the prohibition on advertising abortion procedures themselves.**

The Broadcast Committee of Advertising Practice, or BCAP, has opened the issue as part of a wider review of the codes governing British television and radio advertising. The proposed change would remove the existing distinction between charitable and commercial providers of post-conception advice.

BCAP spokeswoman Lynsay Taffe said: **“We are proposing that all post-conception advice services should be allowed to advertise, provided that they make clear in their ads whether or not they refer women for abortions.”**

Under the proposal, organizations offering counseling and information to pregnant women—including commercial providers as well as charities—could buy broadcast advertising. That could include services run by organizations that also arrange or provide terminations, such as major independent reproductive-health providers, as long as the advertisement promoted pregnancy advice rather than the abortion procedure and clearly disclosed the organization’s referral policy.

The opening would not be limited to organizations supporting abortion rights. Anti-abortion or faith-based pregnancy-counseling organizations could also advertise, subject to the same standards on accuracy, transparency and potential harm. The central requirement would be that viewers or listeners were not misled about whether a service would discuss or arrange abortion.

Taffe emphasized that the proposal should not be interpreted as permission for direct advertising of terminations. **“Abortion clinics themselves would not be allowed to advertise,”** she said.

Clinics devoted solely to carrying out abortions would therefore remain barred from promoting those services on television or radio. Nor would the change permit advertisements for particular abortion methods, prices or procedures. The distinction is between advertising a counseling or post-conception advisory service and advertising abortion as a medical service.

At present, charitable pregnancy-advice organizations may advertise in circumstances in which commercial services generally may not. BCAP’s review is considering whether that difference remains justified, particularly when both types of organization may provide information to women facing an unplanned pregnancy.

Any advertisement approved under the revised system would still have to comply with the broader broadcast codes, including rules against misleading claims and requirements designed to protect children and vulnerable audiences. Regulators would also be able to act if an advertiser concealed its ideological position or falsely suggested that it offered neutral, comprehensive counseling.

The proposals remain subject to consultation and are not an immediate change in the law. Following the consultation and consideration of responses, a revised broadcast code could take effect **toward the end of 2009 at the earliest**, although the timetable could slip depending on the regulator’s final decisions and implementation process.
